text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game: each token kept privately gives me 1 point but costs each of the other three members 0.3, while each token placed in the group account seems to pay only the contributor 0.3 points without directly affecting others—so I'm trying to pin down whether that's really just a transfer or has some multiplier effect.

Running the numbers, if everyone defects fully, each person nets 2 points from tokens (20 kept minus 18 lost from others' defections), but if everyone cooperates fully, each nets 6 points. So mutual cooperation is clearly better for the group, even though keeping tokens privately is the individually dominant strategy since 1 point beats the 0.3 return from contributing. I'm now thinking about how to approach round one given this tension between individual and collective incentives.

For the opening round, since this is a repeated game over 10 rounds, I want to signal cooperative intent and try to establish mutual trust early. I'll contribute the full 20 points to the group account as a cooperative opening move.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure here: keeping a token myself nets me 1 point but costs each of the other three members 0.3 points, while putting a token in the group account only returns 0.3 points to me without affecting the others' points at all.

So individually, keeping is always better (1 > 0.3), making it the dominant strategy, but collectively if everyone keeps, the group ends up worse off than if everyone contributed — a classic social dilemma. Running the numbers: if everyone contributes all 20 tokens, each person ends with 24 points total, but if everyone keeps everything, each ends with only 20 — so full cooperation beats full defection at the group level even though defection dominates individually.

Given this, I'll start by contributing the full 20 tokens in round 1 to signal cooperative intent, treating this like a tit-for-tat approach across the 10 rounds while favoring the socially optimal choice.

Looking at the numbers, my own payoff is maximized by keeping everything private since +1 beats +0.3 individually, making full defection the dominant strategy and Nash equilibrium. Yet collectively, full cooperation yields much higher total payoffs (6 per person vs. 2 per person under full defection), so there's a clear tension between individual incentive and group welfare that repeated play could help resolve.

Given it's a 10-round game, defecting outright risks unraveling cooperation entirely, but committing fully to cooperation first is risky since defectors would gain at my expense. I think starting with a moderate contribution—like putting in 10 out of 20 tokens—is a reasonable way to signal willingness to cooperate while limiting downside exposure.
